title: Case: IoT telemetry with streaming and micro-batches
summary: Fleet telemetry through MQTT and Kafka into Flink alerts, a real-time OLAP store and an Iceberg history, with late events, rollups and retention tiers.

blocks.text: 48.1 Context and requirements

A logistics company operates 50,000 trucks. Each telematics unit sends one message per second with GPS, speed, engine temperature, fuel level and harsh-braking flags: about 50k messages/s, roughly 300 bytes each as JSON, so 15 MB/s or 1.3 TB/day before compression. Units buffer data when coverage drops (tunnels, borders) and replay it later, sometimes days later.

head: Consumer
Need
Latency
rows: Fleet operations
alert on overheating, crash-like braking, device offline
seconds
Control-room dashboards
live map, per-depot KPIs, last 24 h trends
under 1 minute
Analytics and ML
full history for fuel and maintenance models
minutes to hours
Finance and compliance
monthly mileage per vehicle for 5 years
daily

blocks.text: No single engine serves all four well. This is the streaming-first pattern of chapter 45 combined with the OLAP serving of chapter 46 and an Iceberg lake (chapter 42) for history.
48.2 Architecture decision

head: Option
Verdict
rows: A. Everything in a real-time OLAP store
great dashboards, but years of raw history in hot storage is expensive and ML teams want Spark on files
B. Land in the lake, query it for everything
cheap, but minute-level commits cannot drive second-level alerts
C. Kafka as the backbone, three sinks with their own latency: Flink alerts, OLAP store, Iceberg
chosen: each consumer gets the latency it pays for

blocks.title: Architecture decision record
blocks.text:
ADR-031  Fleet telemetry platform                    Status: accepted
Decision: MQTT broker bridges to Kafka (key = device_id). Three readers:
  1. Flink alert job: event-time windows, 5 s watermark, alerts topic.
  2. Real-time OLAP (ClickHouse here): raw 7 days, 1-min rollups 90 days.
  3. Flink Iceberg sink, 5-min checkpoint: raw history 13 months;
     Spark builds hourly rollups kept 5 years.
Consequences: three copies of recent data, each with its own retention;
  Kafka keeps 3 days so any sink can be replayed after an outage.
Revisit if: OLAP store can query Iceberg directly with acceptable latency.

Kafka retention is the recovery budget. If the Iceberg sink is down longer than the topic retention, history is lost; size retention from the longest outage you are willing to survive, not from disk prices.

blocks.title: Retention tiers
blocks.caption: Each tier is a separate table with its own TTL or expiry job, not one table with a lifecycle rule.

blocks.text: 48.4 Data model, time and late events

Every message carries `device_id`, a per-device sequence number `seq`, the device clock `event_time` and the broker-assigned `ingest_time`. Keying Kafka by `device_id` keeps each device's events ordered inside one partition, which makes per-device state and deduplication local (chapter 18).

items: **Duplicates**: MQTT QoS 1 means at-least-once, and buffered replays resend. Deduplicate on `(device_id, seq)` with bounded state (a TTL of hours).
**Out-of-order**: within one device, retries arrive a few seconds late; across devices, clocks drift. A watermark of 5 seconds covers normal jitter (chapter 6).
**Very late**: buffered data arriving hours later is useless for alerts but essential for history. Alerts drop it; OLAP and Iceberg accept it.
**Bad clocks**: a unit with a reset clock reports 1970 or next year. Clamp: if `event_time` is outside `ingest_time` minus 7 days to plus 5 minutes, use `ingest_time` and flag the row.

blocks.text: One idle Kafka partition holds back the watermark of the whole job, so windows never fire at night when part of the fleet is parked. Configure a source idle timeout so idle partitions are excluded from the watermark.

Iceberg bronze is partitioned by `days(event_time)` with `bucket(16, device_id)`, so late events land in old partitions. That is correct but leaves small files in yesterday's partitions, which compaction must revisit (chapter 25).
48.5 Pipelines with code

blocks.title: Flink SQL: event-time alert
blocks.text:
CREATE TABLE telemetry (
  device_id STRING, seq BIGINT, ts_ms BIGINT,
  engine_temp DOUBLE, speed_kmh DOUBLE,
  event_time AS TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(ts_ms, 3),
  WATERMARK FOR event_time AS event_time - INTERVAL '5' SECOND
) WITH (
  'connector' = 'kafka', 'topic' = 'fleet.telemetry',
  'properties.bootstrap.servers' = 'kafka:9092',
  'properties.group.id' = 'alerts', 'format' = 'json');

SET 'table.exec.source.idle-timeout' = '30 s';

INSERT INTO overheat_alerts
SELECT device_id, window_end, avg_temp FROM (
  SELECT device_id, window_start, window_end, AVG(engine_temp) AS avg_temp
  FROM TABLE(TUMBLE(TABLE telemetry, DESCRIPTOR(event_time),
                    INTERVAL '10' SECOND))
  GROUP BY device_id, window_start, window_end)
WHERE avg_temp > 110;

The alert fires when the watermark passes the window end: worst case 10 s of window plus 5 s of watermark delay, plus processing. Shrinking either lowers latency and raises noise or dropped late events. Device-offline detection is the absence of events, which needs per-key timers; it is usually written as a `KeyedProcessFunction` in the DataStream API rather than SQL (chapter 20).

blocks.title: ClickHouse SQL: raw table and rollup
blocks.text:
CREATE TABLE telemetry_raw (
  device_id String, event_time DateTime64(3),
  engine_temp Float32, speed_kmh Float32
) ENGINE = MergeTree
PARTITION BY toDate(event_time)
ORDER BY (device_id, event_time)
TTL toDateTime(event_time) + INTERVAL 7 DAY;

CREATE TABLE telemetry_1m (
  device_id String, minute DateTime,
  temp_avg AggregateFunction(avg, Float32),
  temp_max AggregateFunction(max, Float32),
  speed_max AggregateFunction(max, Float32)
) ENGINE = AggregatingMergeTree
ORDER BY (device_id, minute)
TTL minute + INTERVAL 90 DAY;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW telemetry_1m_mv TO telemetry_1m AS
SELECT device_id, toStartOfMinute(event_time) AS minute,
       avgState(engine_temp) AS temp_avg, maxState(engine_temp) AS temp_max,
       maxState(speed_kmh) AS speed_max
FROM telemetry_raw GROUP BY device_id, minute;

-- query: SELECT minute, avgMerge(temp_avg), maxMerge(temp_max)
--        FROM telemetry_1m WHERE device_id = 'T-1042' GROUP BY minute;

The rollup stores partial aggregation *states*, not final numbers, so a late event inserted tomorrow simply adds another state that merges correctly. Keep `max` and `min`, not only `avg`: an average over a minute hides the 3-second temperature spike the maintenance team cares about.

blocks.title: Spark SQL: hourly rollup recomputing the last 3 days
blocks.text:
INSERT OVERWRITE lake.gold.telemetry_hourly
SELECT device_id, date_trunc('hour', event_time) AS hour,
       avg(engine_temp) AS temp_avg, max(engine_temp) AS temp_max,
       max(speed_kmh) AS speed_max, count(*) AS samples
FROM lake.bronze.telemetry
WHERE event_time >= date_sub(current_date(), 3)
GROUP BY device_id, date_trunc('hour', event_time);

With dynamic partition overwrite (`spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode=dynamic`) and the table partitioned by `days(hour)`, each run replaces only the days it recomputes, so late data arriving within 3 days is absorbed. Data later than that is caught by a weekly job that recomputes days whose bronze partitions received new files, found from Iceberg metadata tables.
48.6 Operations, cost and failure modes

head: Item
Order of magnitude
Lever
rows: Kafka
1.3 TB/day raw; 3 days x RF 3 is about 12 TB before compression
zstd producer compression, binary encoding (Avro/Protobuf)
Iceberg raw
roughly 70-130 GB/day as Parquet, tens of TB over 13 months
sorted by device and time for compression; expiry job

blocks.text: The numbers are estimates for planning, not quotes; the shape matters more: raw volume is dominated by the warm tier, query cost by the hot tier, and fixed cost by always-on Kafka and Flink.

items: **Watermark stall**: idle partitions or one device with a future clock (if not clamped) freeze or jump the watermark.
**Alert storms**: a firmware bug sends temperature 255 from 5,000 units; deduplicate alerts per device and route them through a rate limiter.
**Hot partitions**: a few gateway devices aggregate hundreds of sensors under one key; key by sensor or add a salt.
**Small files**: 5-minute commits into 16 buckets for today and late days; compact daily and after backfills.
**Silent schema change**: new firmware renames a field; fields arrive null. Contract the payload with a schema registry and alert on null ratios (chapter 33).

blocks.title: Border backlog
blocks.text: 200 trucks cross a border with no roaming for 6 hours and then upload 4 million buffered events in 10 minutes.
items: Alert job: events are behind the watermark and dropped from windows, by design; a side output counts them.
OLAP: rows insert into old minutes; the rollup states merge and the dashboards correct themselves.
Iceberg: rows append to the right day; the next hourly run recomputes the affected hours.

blocks.title: Add geofence events
blocks.text: Operations wants an event when a truck enters or leaves one of 3,000 depot polygons, within 10 seconds, plus a monthly report of dwell time per depot that must be exact even with late data. Design the stream job, the storage and the recomputation strategy.
hints: Is entering a geofence a window aggregate or per-device state?
Which store answers 'trucks currently in depot X' and which one answers the monthly report?
How do very late GPS points change a dwell time that was already reported?

items: One Kafka backbone feeds sinks with different latencies: Flink for seconds, OLAP for dashboards, Iceberg for history.
Watermarks trade latency for completeness; idle partitions must be excluded or windows stall.
Deduplicate on device id plus sequence; clamp impossible device clocks.
Rollups keep min, max, count and aggregation states so late data merges correctly.
Retention tiers are separate tables with their own TTL: hot raw days, hot rollups months, warm raw a year, cold rollups years.
Kafka retention is the replay budget for any failed sink.

blocks.q: Alerts stop firing every night although trucks are still driving. What is the most likely cause?
options: The tumbling window is too short
ClickHouse TTL deleted the raw data
Idle Kafka partitions from parked trucks hold back the job's watermark
blocks.explain: The watermark is the minimum across partitions; an idle one stops it. Window size changes latency, not whether windows fire.

blocks.q: Why does the 1-minute rollup store `avgState` instead of a final average?
options: Late rows add new states that merge correctly with existing ones
ClickHouse cannot compute averages in materialized views
It uses less disk than a float
blocks.explain: Partial states are mergeable, so late inserts correct the minute. A stored final average could not absorb a new row without the original count.

blocks.q: Buffered data arrives 6 hours late. Which statement is correct for this design?
options: Iceberg rewrites the whole table to insert it
Kafka rejects it because it is older than the retention
The alert job drops it from windows, while OLAP and Iceberg store it in the right time buckets
All three sinks drop it because it is behind the watermark
blocks.explain: Only the windowed alert job drops late events. Kafka retention uses the record timestamp, normally set when the bridge produces it, not the device clock.

blocks.q: What best determines Kafka topic retention here?
options: The longest sink outage you must recover from by replay
The size of the OLAP store's disks
blocks.explain: Retention is the replay window for every downstream sink; disk price is a constraint, not the driver.
